## Methods

Materials
Polyvinyl alcohol (PVA, Mw 89000-98000, 98-99% hydrolyzed), vanadium pentoxide (V2O5, ≥99.5%), aniline (≥99.5%), ammonium metavanadate (NH4VO3, ≥99%), N-Methylpyrrolidone (NMP, ≥99.5%), ammonium persulfate (APS, ≥98%), and N,N’-methylenebisacrylamide (MBAA, ≥99%) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Bio-Chem Technology Co. Ltd. Zinc acetate dihydrate (CH3COO)2Zn·2H2O (98%), ethylene glycol (EG, 98%), phosphoric acid (H3PO4, ≥85 wt.% in H2O, ≥99.99% metals basis), potassium sulfate (K2SO4, 99%), isopropanol (≥99%), ethanol (>99.9%), Iron(III) nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, 99.9%) and acrylic acid (>99%) was purchased from Shanghai Macleans Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. Oxalic acid (H2C2O4·2H2O, ≥99.5%) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2, ≥30%) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Zinc trifluoromethanesulfonate (Zn(OTf)2, 98%) was purchased from Energy Chemical. Super P (>99.9%) was purchased from Feynman Biotechnology Tech Co., Ltd. Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF, average Mw ~1,100,000, ≥99.5%) was purchased from Nanjing Moges Energy Technology Co., Ltd. Silver nanoflakes (96.5%) was purchased from Jiangsu XFNANO Materials Tech Co., Ltd. Zinc plate (99.99%) was purchased from Chengshuo Metal Materials Co., Ltd., and deionized water was used for all experiments.

Preparation of electrode materials
Synthesis of Zn3V3O8. To synthesize the negative electrode host materials62, 10 mmol of (CH3COO)2Zn·2H2O and 10 mmol of NH4VO3 were added to 60 mL of deionized water and stirred magnetically at 90°C for 5.5 h to form a sol. The sol was then dried in an oven at 70°C for 72 h. After drying, the obtained bulk product was ground into a fine powder and annealed at 750°C for 9 h under a 5% Ar/H2 mixed gas atmosphere with a heating rate of 4°C min−1, then cooled naturally to obtain the target product.

Synthesis of layered NH4V4O10. To synthesize the positive electrode host materials63, 4.67 mmol of NH4VO3 and 0.71 mmol of H2C2O4·2H2O were dissolved in 70 mL of distilled water and stirred at 25°C for 1 h. The solution was then transferred to a hydrothermal autoclave and heated at 180°C for 2 h. After the reaction, the product was naturally cooled to 25°C, washed sequentially with deionized water and ethanol three times, and dried at 60°C to yield the target product.

Synthesis of VOP and PA-VOP. To synthesize VOP64, 2.4 g of V2O5 powder and 13.3 mL of H3PO4 were added to 57.7 mL of deionized water and stirred for 2 h. The mixture was then heated in a hydrothermal reactor at 120°C for 16 h. After the reaction, the product was centrifuged, washed, and dried at 60°C to obtain VOP.

Subsequently, PA-VOP was synthesized using an ultrasonic exfoliation and self-assembly process. For this, 100 mg of VOPO4 powder was dispersed in 7 mL of isopropanol, and the solution was sonicated for 30 min. After centrifugation, the exfoliated sheets were transferred into an aniline solvent and stirred for 24 h. The product was then centrifuged, washed, and dried under vacuum at 60°C.

Synthesis of KVOH and VOH. To synthesize KVOH65, 0.364 g of V2O5 was dissolved in 50 mL of deionized water, and 2 mL of H2O2 was added. Separately, 0.087 g of K2SO4 was dissolved in 30 mL of deionized water. The two solutions were mixed under magnetic stirring for 0.5 h and then heated at 120°C for 6 h. The resulting precipitate was washed three times with deionized water and ethanol and dried in an oven at 60°C to obtain the green powder KVOH. For VOH, the same procedure was followed without adding K2SO4.

Fabrication of hydrogel electrolytes and testing electrodes
To prepare the electrolyte56, 4.5 g of polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) powder was added to 40 mL of a mixed solution containing 1 M Zn(OTf)2 in water and ethylene glycol. The mixture was stirred at 90°C until it dissolved uniformly and then froze at −40°C for crosslinking to form the hydrogel.

For the testing electrode, the electrode slurry was formulated by thoroughly mixing the active material (lab-synthesized), Super P, and PVDF in a mass ratio of 7:2:1 within NMP solvent. This slurry was then manually single-side coated onto the titanium mesh (99.99%, 200 meshes, thickness: 0.5 mm, pore size: 0.077 mm) utilizing a coating brush. Following drying under 60°C, the electrode sheets were punched into circular disks with an electrode cutter (MSK-T10, Shenzhen Kejing Star Technology Co., Ltd.), achieving a targeted active material mass loading of 1–2 mg cm−2. Notably, the basic electrochemical performance of the electrode materials was tested by assembling coin cells (CR2032, 20×20×3 mm, stainless steel 304) with electrode sheets (φ=12 mm) and hydrogel electrolytes (φ=16 mm, volume: 0.26±0.05 cm3). For the half-cell test, zinc foil (thickness: 80 μm) was used as the negative electrode.

Fabrication of hydrogel electrodes and assembled AZIBs
A precursor solution was prepared with ethylene glycol and water in a 2:1 volume ratio, followed by the addition of 15 mL of acrylic acid to 35 mL of the mixed solution. To this, 150 mg of Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, 20 mg of MBAA, and 150 mg of APS were added. The mixture was stirred thoroughly, and ethanol (50 vol% relative to the total precursor volume) was added to retard the spontaneous polymerization process, yielding the polyacrylic acid (PAA) precursor solution.

The hydrogel electrodes were formulated by homogeneously mixing active electrode material (NH4V4O10 for the positive electrode or Zn3V3O8 for the negative electrode) with Ag nanoflakes in the PAA hydrogel precursor solution. The concentration of the active material was systematically varied from 60 to 300 mg mL−1, while the concentration of Ag nanoflakes was maintained constant at 400 mg mL−1 to ensure consistent electrical conductivity. The resulting mixtures were poured into Petri dishes and gelled at 60°C to form self-supporting electrode films with a uniform thickness of approximately 0.1 mm. These freestanding hydrogel electrodes were then cut into rectangular strips of desired dimensions (typically 10 mm×25 mm) using a surgical blade. The electrolyte and substrate consisted of the PVA hydrogel, prepared according to the procedure described in the previous section of hydrogel electrolyte. The PVA precursor solution was cast in a Petri dish and gelled at −40°C, forming a transparent, freestanding film with a thickness of approximately 1.0 mm. A coplanar battery architecture was constructed by arranging the discrete positive and negative hydrogel electrode strips in parallel on the same PVA hydrogel substrate, maintaining a defined insulating gap of 0.2 mm between them to prevent internal short-circuiting. The assembly was fully encapsulated by casting a second layer of PVA precursor solution over the electrodes and substrate, followed by a final gelling step at −40°C. This created a monolithic, all-hydrogel structure with integrated ionic continuity. External electrical connections were established by attaching flexible conductive adhesive tapes to the exposed terminals of the hydrogel electrodes, enabling electrochemical testing and the configuration of devices in series. The electrochemical properties of the electrodes were evaluated using CV, GCD, and EIS methods via an electrochemical workstation. Additionally, the mechanical properties of the hydrogel electrodes were measured and compared using a universal testing machine.

Characterizations
SEM was performed on a Sirion sweep electron microscope (FEI, Hillsboro, USA) with a 20 kV working voltage. The element valence of the electrode samples was analyzed by XPS on a 4800X X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (Thermo Fisher, Waltham, USA). XRD curves were recorded using a DX-2700b X-ray diffractometer (XRD) (Haoyuan Instrument, Dandong, China) with Cu-Kα radiation at a step interval of 0.02° and a scanning speed of 8° min−1. The tensile and compression properties of hydrogel samples were measured using an MTS Universal Testing Machine (E43, Shenzhen, China). The electrochemical experiments were performed using a Biologic VSP workstation (Seyssinet-Pariset, France) in an ambient laboratory environment maintained at 25°C (no climatic/environmental chamber), while a CT2001A LAND battery test system (Wuhan, China) was used for galvanostatic charge-discharge testing at 25°C. EIS measurements were carried out using a potentiostatic signal with an amplitude of 10 mV. The frequency was swept from 100 kHz down to 100 mHz with an acquisition density of 6 points per decade. To ensure the measurements were carried out under a quasi-stationary state, the cells were left at open circuit for 30 min to reach a stable potential before the initiation of each frequency sweep. For ex situ analysis (XPS/XRD), cycled electrodes were harvested under ambient laboratory conditions (~25°C, air environment). The working electrode (slurry-coated titanium mesh) was carefully extracted from the electrochemical cell after reaching the target potential during galvanostatic cycling (1 Ag−1 in 1 M Zn(CF3SO3)2 aqueous electrolyte, with Zn metal or a compatible electrode as the counter electrode). The harvested electrode was immediately rinsed with anhydrous ethanol to remove residual electrolyte salts, followed by drying in air. The dried samples were stored in sealed containers under ambient conditions prior to analysis. All ex situ measurements were performed under controlled temperature conditions (25°C).

Density functional simulation
First-principles calculations based on density functional theory (DFT) were performed using the Vienna Ab-initio Simulation Package with projector-augmented wave pseudopotentials66. The exchange-correlation interactions were treated within the generalized gradient approximation using the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof functional67,68. A plane-wave energy cutoff of 500 eV was employed, and the Brillouin zone was sampled with a 3×3×3 k-point mesh. The electronic energy convergence criterion was set to 10−7 eV, while structural relaxations were performed until the maximum Hellmann-Feynman force on each atom was reduced below 0.005 eV Å−1. The nudged elastic band method was used to evaluate diffusion energy barriers69.

Finite element simulation
Finite element simulations were conducted using COMSOL Multiphysics 6.2 to investigate ion concentration profiles and the spatial distribution of the electric field within a dual-intercalation battery system. The simulation framework integrated the “Battery Module” and the “Transport of Diluted Species” interfaces in a coupled approach. Ion insertion and extraction at the electrode surfaces were governed by the Butler-Volmer kinetics, while ion diffusion within both the positive and negative electrode was modeled according to Fick’s law. In the electrolyte phase, ion migration under the influence of an electric field was described using the Nernst-Planck equation. For the simulation, the Zn2+ diffusion coefficients in the positive electrode were set to 1.0×10−11 m2 s−1 for the control group and 1.0×10−10 m2 s−1 for the experimental group. The initial Zn2+ ion concentration in the electrolyte was 1000 mol m−3. A constant charging current of 0.006 A was applied, with a maximum voltage limit of 1.8 V.

Machine learning implementation
An XGBoost model was employed to predict the electrochemical performance of dual-intercalation AZIBs based on diffusion-derived descriptors. The training dataset was obtained exclusively from experimentally measured data in this study. To quantitatively assess kinetic compatibility between electrode pairs, two key descriptors were defined: the CSI and the DR. CSI quantifies the divergence in ion diffusion kinetics between electrodes, reflecting the degree of synchronization in their intercalation behavior. DR is defined as the ratio of the mean apparent ion diffusion coefficients (logarithmic values) of the positive and negative electrode, providing a scale-invariant measure of relative diffusion rates. The respective formulas for calculating these descriptors are provided below:

CSI = |lgD+ - lgD-| + 2 * |σlgD+ - σlgD-| / (lgD+ * lgD-)

DR = lgD+ / lgD-

Where lgD+ and lgD- denote the logarithmic value of the zinc ion diffusion coefficient of positive and negative electrode at each step of the charge-discharge process. ### Reviewer 2

The authors of this study sought to address the mismatch in ion diffusion rates between the cathode and anode, which is a
key cause of performance degradation in aqueous zinc-ion batteries. To this end, they introduced a machine learning
approach and, for the first time, developed a “kinetic matching model” capable of quantitatively predicting the kinetic
compatibility of two electrodes. Using this model, they identified the optimal electrode pairing (ZVO||NVO) and successfully
fabricated a battery with an outstanding lifespan of over 12,000 cycles. Furthermore, they applied this principle to hydrogel-
based flexible batteries, achieving both high energy density and mechanical stability. Ultimately, this work presents a new
paradigm for data-driven, rational battery design. However, additional revisions addressing the following major questions
are necessary for publication in Nature Communications.
1. In the DFT-based NEB calculations, it is unclear why only NVO-1 exhibits migration along a different crystallographic
direction. It would be beneficial to also provide results in which all migration paths are aligned along the same direction for
consistency. Furthermore, while it is stated that the Bader charge results are related to the diffusion barrier, the explanation
does not clearly specify whose charge variation is responsible for this correlation.
2. The strategy of optimizing the kinetics by lowering the upper cut-off voltage from 2.0 V to 1.8 V is highly original. However,
this approach directly sacrifices the battery’s energy density (Energy = Capacity × Voltage). While the 1.8 V cell may exhibit
superior rate capability and cycle life, a quantitative comparison is needed to determine how much energy density is lost
compared to the 2.0 V cell. From a practical application standpoint, where is the balance point between the benefits of
improved lifespan and rate performance and the drawbacks of reduced energy density? Furthermore, can the current model
also assist in identifying this optimal practical trade-off?
3. In Fig. 5f, the optimal ranges of DR and CSI are determined based on a threshold of the “top 30%.” However, this “top
30%” criterion may appear somewhat arbitrary. Have you examined how sensitive the proposed optimal design range
(design rule) is to changes in this threshold, for example, if it were set to the “top 10%” or “top 50%”? If the robustness of this
design rule is strongly dependent on the chosen threshold, wouldn’t that limit its general applicability?
4. In Li-ion batteries, it is common practice to intentionally design the anode capacity to be greater than that of the cathode in
order to prevent critical issues such as lithium metal plating. In the dual-insertion system studied here, is pursuing perfectly
symmetric kinetics (DR ≈ 1) always the optimal approach? Would it not be more stable and robust to intentionally design the
anode kinetics to be slightly faster than the cathode, so that it can serve as a “buffer” to accommodate the incoming ion flux
from the cathode during sudden high-power demands? Could the model’s optimal DR range of 0.936–1.020, which is not
perfectly symmetric around 1.0, be hinting at the necessity of such asymmetry?
5. The CSI and DR proposed in this study are highly effective features designed based on deep physical insights into battery
kinetics. However, they represent a successful case of “feature engineering” grounded in the researchers’ expertise, rather
than features “learned” or “generated” autonomously by AI. Certain expressions in the manuscript (e.g., “ML-based model”)
could be interpreted as implying that AI itself is the agent explaining this phenomenon. Would it not convey the
methodological essence more accurately to clearly redefine the role of AI in this work as “a powerful statistical tool for
validating the hypotheses of the researcher-proposed physical model and modeling complex nonlinear relationships”?
6. It would be helpful to include in the Supporting Information the results of tests conducted using several other machine
learning methods.

(7) If the anode is metallic zinc, NVO undergoes changes during charging and
discharging. Therefore, it is difficult to attribute the fast kinetics solely to spacing
modification, given the presence of Zn intercalation, as you mentioned. More precisely,
the interlayer spacing of NVO can be effectively modulated by adjusting the zinc ion
intercalation rather than by altering the charge-discharge cut-off voltage.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the insightful comment regarding the origin of
fast kinetics in NVO cathodes. The interlayer spacing of NVO is dynamically
modulated by the intercalation and deintercalation of both Zn2+ and NH₄+ ions during
charge-discharge cycling, resulting in a distribution of diffusion barriers rather than a
single fixed value and reflecting variable ion transport pathways within the layered
structure. By adjusting the cut-off voltage, the upper and lower bounds of this spacing
variation can be effectively controlled, tailoring the distribution of Zn2+ diffusion rates
and optimizing overall ion transport kinetics. This approach enables practical
modulation of kinetic behavior without altering the intrinsic crystal structure, providing
a flexible strategy to achieve fast charge-discharge performance. While other methods,
such as varying reaction temperature, tuning the hydrated radius of Zn2+, or adjusting
the applied cell voltage, can influence ion transport, they generally affect the system
globally and cannot selectively balance the kinetic mismatch between cathode and
anode. Targeted interventions, including artificial SEI layers, increasing intercalation
site density, or surface morphology engineering, can finely regulate Zn2+ kinetics for a
specific electrode, but these approaches are electrode-specific and lack general
applicability. In contrast, controlling the interlayer spacing via the cut-off voltage
provides a relatively universal and practical strategy: by tuning the voltage, the extent
of layer expansion or contraction can be freely adjusted, directly influencing
intercalation pathways and surface ion flux, allowing controlled amplification or
suppression of Zn2+ diffusion kinetics and enabling kinetic matching across electrodes.
Importantly, this dynamic interlayer adjustment also enhances structural stability. As
the spacing adapts to accommodate Zn2+ ions, lattice strain is minimized, reducing the
risk of layer collapse or mechanical degradation during cycling. The reversible
expansion and contraction facilitate fast, reversible Zn2+ intercalation and
deintercalation, explaining the observed high-rate capability. This dual effect, enhanced
kinetics and improved structural robustness, demonstrates that cut-off voltage control
is an effective and practical means to tune both performance and durability in NVO-
based aqueous zinc-ion batteries. Following the reviewer’s advice, we have added the
relevant discussion into the Results and Discussion sections on Page 10, Line 10 in
the revised manuscript, as shown below:

of interlayer spacing variation, directly tuning Zn2+ diffusion pathways and surface flux.

KVOH and VOP vs. PA-VOP, which revealed highly similar redox peak positions and
only moderate differences in capacity relative to the full-cell measurements. This
indicates that intercalation modification did not fundamentally alter the charge storage

inserted is minimal and contributes negligibly to the overall capacity. Importantly, the
observed shifts in redox peaks in Figure 4d are consistent with enhanced zinc-ion
diffusion kinetics due to interlayer expansion and improved anode-cathode matching,
rather than significant proton contributions. Therefore, the enhanced electrochemical

Comments:
The authors of this study sought to address the mismatch in ion diffusion rates
between the cathode and anode, which is a key cause of performance degradation in
aqueous zinc-ion batteries. To this end, they introduced a machine learning approach
and, for the first time, developed a “kinetic matching model ” capable of
quantitatively predicting the kinetic compatibility of two electrodes. Using this model,
they identified the optimal electrode pairing (ZVO||NVO) and successfully fabricated
a battery with an outstanding lifespan of over 12,000 cycles. Furthermore, they applied
this principle to hydrogel-based flexible batteries, achieving both high energy density
and mechanical stability. Ultimately, this work presents a new paradigm for data-driven,

Response: We appreciate the comments from reviewer, and we have tried our best to

(1) In the DFT-based NEB calculations, it is unclear why only NVO-1 exhibits
migration along a different crystallographic direction. It would be beneficial to also
provide results in which all migration paths are aligned along the same direction for
consistency. Furthermore, while it is stated that the Bader charge results are related to
the diffusion barrier, the explanation does not clearly specify whose charge variation is
responsible for this correlation.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these insightful comments regarding the DFT-
based NEB calculations. Regarding the first point, the migration path of Zn2+ ions is
intrinsically dictated by the most favorable adsorption sites within each NVO structure.
In NVO-2, NVO-3, and NVO-4, the existence of NH₄+ vacancies creates low-energy
adsorption centers, guiding Zn2+ diffusion along vacancy-vacancy pathways. By
contrast, NVO-1 lacks intrinsic vacancies, and therefore, we systematically evaluated
multiple potential adsorption configurations. Four distinct adsorption sites (denoted A,
B, C, and D) were identified, with calculated adsorption energies of –2.130 eV, –0.163
eV, –1.347 eV, and –2.130 eV, respectively. Among these, sites A and D are symmetry-
equivalent and correspond to the most stable adsorption states. Consequently, the A→D
pathway was selected for NEB analysis, as it minimizes the migration barrier. For
comparison, we also examined an alternative pathway (A→C), which aligns more
closely with the migration direction observed in other NVO samples. However, as
shown in Fig. S2, Path-1 (A→D) yields a substantially lower diffusion barrier than
Path-2 (A→C), confirming that enforcing the same crystallographic direction as other
NVOs would artificially overestimate the barrier. Thus, the reported NVO-1 pathway
reflects the most energetically realistic migration route.
Regarding the second point, the Bader charge analysis specifically refers to the charge
transfer associated with the Zn2+ ion when occupying different adsorption sites. A lower
absolute Bader charge value indicates more effective charge stabilization at the
adsorption site, which weakens the electrostatic interaction between Zn2+ and the host
lattice. This stabilization directly correlates with a reduced diffusion barrier, as the Zn2+
ion encounters less resistance during migration. We have revised the manuscript to
explicitly clarify that the Zn2+ charge variation, rather than changes in the host
framework, underpins the observed correlation between Bader charge values and
diffusion barriers.
Following this, the relevant discussion has been added into the Results and Discussion
sections on Page 8, Line 15 and Line 28 in the revised manuscript and Page 2 in the
Supporting Information, as shown below:

“For NVO-2, NVO-3, and NVO-4, diffusion energy barriers were calculated using the
most stable adsorption site at the ammonium vacancy. For NVO-1, which lacks intrinsic
vacancies, multiple adsorption configurations were evaluated (Figure S2), and the
configuration with the lowest adsorption energy was selected to ensure accurate
diffusion barrier determination. Comparative analysis of two possible diffusion paths,
Path-1 and Path-2, revealed that Path-1 exhibits a lower Zn2+ diffusion barrier,
confirming it as the most favorable diffusion pathway. These calculations ensure that
the reported barriers accurately reflect the energetically preferred ion transport routes.”

(2) The strategy of optimizing the kinetics by lowering the upper cut-off voltage from

trade-off between kinetic optimization and energy density resulting from the reduced
upper cut-off voltage. Indeed, lowering the voltage window from 2.0 V to 1.8 V
inevitably reduces the nominal energy density (Energy = Capacity × Voltage). However,
as shown in Figure 3c, the discharge plateau (reduction peak) remains largely
unchanged, which means the actual loss is less pronounced than might be expected from

incurring an energy density loss of approximately 15.4-19.1%. By contrast, at higher
current densities, the 1.8 V cell achieves superior energy density, as the improved
kinetics and reduced polarization enable more efficient utilization of the active material.

dependent: for energy-oriented applications, a wider voltage window is preferable,
while for high-power applications, the 1.8 V configuration offers a better overall
compromise between energy, power, and long-term stability. Importantly, the modeling
framework developed in this study can be extended to systematically identify such
balance points for different electrode systems, thereby serving as a practical tool to
guide optimization of energy-power trade-offs in Zn-metal-free systems. Following this,

(4) In Li-ion batteries, it is common practice to intentionally design the anode capacity
to be greater than that of the cathode in order to prevent critical issues such as lithium
metal plating. In the dual-insertion system studied here, is pursuing perfectly
symmetric kinetics (DR ≈ 1) always the optimal approach? Would it not be more stable and robust to intentionally design the
anode kinetics to be slightly faster than the cathode, so that it can serve as a “buffer” to accommodate the incoming ion flux

perfectly symmetric around 1.0, be hinting at the necessity of such asymmetry?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this insightful point regarding
the potential advantage of intentionally asymmetric kinetics. Indeed, in conventional
Li-ion batteries, anode overmatching is often employed as a safety buffer to prevent
lithium plating. However, in the dual-intercalation aqueous zinc-ion system studied
here, both electrodes operate via intercalation, and Zn2+ transport is inherently slower
than Li+. Therefore, maintaining close kinetic synchrony between the anode and
cathode is crucial, as a significant mismatch in diffusion rates at either electrode would
create a rate-limiting bottleneck, limiting overall cell performance, as conceptually
illustrated in Figure 1.
The machine-learning-derived optimal DR range (0.936-1.020) is tightly centered near
unity, reflecting this principle of kinetic balance. The slight asymmetry of the range,
as noted by the reviewer, may indeed hint at a modest tolerance for slightly faster anode
kinetics. This bias arises naturally from the composition of the training dataset: the
anode materials generally exhibit higher diffusion rates than the cathodes, leading to a
small skew in DR values below 1, as shown in Supplementary Table S3g. Thus, while
the model accommodates minor asymmetry, the overarching design guideline remains
the achievement of well-matched intercalation kinetics to ensure efficient ion flux,
minimize polarization, and maximize rate capability and cycling stability in dual-
intercalation AZIBs. The corresponding discussion is presented on Page 3, Line 38 and

(4) The manuscript alludes to "cathode-anode kinetic mismatch" but does not clearly
explain how this mismatch leads to performance degradation. A brief mechanistic
explanation would strengthen the argument for kinetic matching.
Response: We thank the reviewer for prompting a more detailed mechanistic
explanation of how cathode-anode kinetic mismatch contributes to performance
degradation. Kinetic mismatch occurs when the intercalation/deintercalation rates of
Zn²⁺ ions in the cathode and anode are misaligned. If the cathode’s deintercalation is
faster than the anode’s intercalation, Zn2+ accumulates at the anode-electrolyte interface
during charging, causing localized concentration polarization. Conversely, if the
cathode intercalates more slowly than the anode deintercalates, ion congestion builds
at the cathode-electrolyte interface during discharge. Such mismatches distort the
electric field distribution, increasing the overpotential required for ion migration and
elevating overall cell polarization. This manifests experimentally as voltage hysteresis,
CV peak separation, and asymmetric current responses, ultimately reducing energy
efficiency, accelerating capacity fade, and limiting rate capability. In contrast, well-
matched kinetics ensure synchronous ion flux, maintain interfacial equilibrium,
promote uniform electric field distribution, and minimize polarization, thereby
enhancing reversibility, rate performance, and cycling stability. Following this, the
relevant discussion has been added into the Results and Discussion sections on Page
6, Line 27 in the revised manuscript, as shown below:
Page 6
“The kinetic mismatch between the electrodes leads to asynchronous ion intercalation
and deintercalation processes. When the cathode deintercalates faster than the anode
can intercalate, Zn2+ accumulates at the anode-electrolyte interface; conversely, slower
cathode intercalation relative to anode deintercalation causes ion congestion at the
cathode-electrolyte interface. These local imbalances distort the uniform electric field
within the cell, requiring higher overpotentials to drive ion migration and increasing
overall polarization. Electrochemically, this manifests as voltage hysteresis, peak
splitting in cyclic voltammetry, and asymmetric current responses, reflecting inefficient
redox reactions and compromised kinetics. Quantitative kinetic matching mitigates
these effects by synchronizing ion flux, stabilizing interfacial conditions, and
minimizing polarization, thereby improving rate performance, energy efficiency, and
long-term cycling stability.”
